extraction.name: FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark
extraction.description: FLORES-101 is an evaluation benchmark for low-resource and multilingual machine translation, consisting of 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage) and professionally translated into 101 languages. The dataset enables many-to-many multilingual translation evaluation across 10,100 language pairs, with rich metadata supporting document-level and multimodal translation evaluation.
extraction.creator: Facebook AI Research (FAIR) and LORIA
extraction.inLanguage: 101 languages including Afrikaans, Amharic, Arabic, Armenian, Assamese, Asturian, Azerbaijani, Belarusian, Bengali, Bosnian, Bulgarian, Burmese, Catalan, Cebuano, Chinese (Simplified), Chinese (Traditional), Croatian, Czech, Danish, Dutch, Estonian, Filipino (Tagalog), Finnish, French, Fula, Galician, Ganda, Georgian, German, Greek, Gujarati, Hausa, Hebrew, Hindi, Hungarian, Icelandic, Igbo, Indonesian, Irish, Italian, Japanese, Javanese, Kabuverdianu, Kamba, Kannada, Kazakh, Khmer, Korean, Kyrgyz, Lao, Latvian, Lingala, Lithuanian, Luo, Luxembourgish, Macedonian, Malay, Malayalam, Maltese, Maori, Marathi, Mongolian, Nepali, Northern Sotho, Norwegian, Nyanja, Occitan, Oriya, Oromo, Pashto, Persian, Polish, Portuguese (Brazil), Punjabi, Romanian, Russian, Serbian, Shona, Sindhi, Slovak, Slovenian, Somali, Sorani Kurdish, Spanish (Latin America), Swahili, Swedish, Tajik, Tamil, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Umbundu, Urdu, Uzbek, Vietnamese, Welsh, Wolof, Xhosa, Yoruba, Chinese, Zulu
extraction.citeAs: Naman Goyal, Cynthia Gao, Vishrav Chaudhary, Peng-Jen Chen, Guillaume Wenzek, Da Ju, Sanjana Krishnan, Marc'Aurelio Ranzato, Francisco Guzmán, Angela Fan. The FLORES-101 Evaluation Benchmark for Low-Resource and Multilingual Machine Translation. arXiv:2106.03193v1 [cs.CL], 6 Jun 2021.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Sentences were extracted from English Wikipedia sources (Wikinews, Wikijunior, and WikiVoyage) covering a variety of topics and domains. Articles were selected at random from each source, and then 3-5 contiguous sentences were manually selected from each article. The selection process was performed by 10 different annotators. Sentences were then professionally translated into 101 languages through a carefully controlled process involving Language Service Providers (LSPs) with multiple rounds of translation, automatic quality checks, and human quality assurance.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Source sentences were extracted from three English Wikimedia sources: Wikinews (international news articles), Wikijunior (age-appropriate nonfiction books for children), and WikiVoyage (travel guide articles). Approximately one third of sentences came from each source.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Sentences were selected by choosing one paragraph per document from either the beginning, middle, or end of the article, with balanced distribution across the corpus. Each sentence was labeled with metadata including Wikipedia URL, topic, boolean flags for hyperlinked entities and images, and a sub-topic classification (one of 10 categories: crime, disasters, entertainment, geography, health, nature, politics, science, sports, travel).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Automatic quality checks were applied to translations including: (i) language identification, (ii) checking whether the translation is a copy of the source sentence, (iii) checking whether the translation has significantly different length, (iv) checking translation fluency according to a language model, and (v) checking whether the translation is a copy of translations produced by publicly available translation engines. Translations with more than 10% of sentences violating the copy-detection criteria were required to be re-translated. A heuristic based on sentence-level SentencePiece BLEU (spBLEU) was used to detect and reject translations likely copied from translation engines.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Sentences were translated by professional translators through Language Service Providers (LSPs). The workflow involved: (1) translation by an initial LSP including editing, (2) automated quality control checks, (3) human quality assurance by an independent LSP using a Translation Quality Score (0-100 scale) based on identified errors in grammar, punctuation, spelling, capitalization, addition/omission, mistranslation, unnatural translation, untranslated text, and register, each with severity levels (minor, major, critical). Translations scoring below 90% were sent back for re-translation. Two pilot experiments were conducted to determine the best LSPs and workflow. The final workflow used was A-C-A (same LSP handles translation and re-translation, independent LSP handles quality assurance).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Language Service Providers (LSPs) - external professional translation and quality assurance agencies
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Translation quality was assessed using a Translation Quality Score on a 0-100 scale. All 101 languages in FLORES-101 meet the threshold of 90% quality based on human evaluation. About 50% of languages have quality scores above 95%. 45 languages required re-translation, with an average of 1 re-translation and a maximum of 3. The most common error category was mistranslation. No clear trend was found across domains in terms of error rates.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dev and devtest splits are publicly downloadable. The test set is available only through a publicly available evaluation server to guarantee equivalent assessment and reduce overfitting. The authors expressed intent to continue expanding the number of languages covered in FLORES-101 and make the test set available to community evaluation campaigns such as WMT shared tasks.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: FLORES-101 aims to foster progress in machine translation for low-resource languages, which are spoken by the majority of the world's population. By enabling evaluation of many-to-many multilingual translation including regionally-relevant language pairs (e.g., Spanish-Aymara, Vietnamese-Thai, Xhosa-Zulu), the benchmark supports development of translation systems that can benefit speakers of underrepresented languages. The dataset also supports non-English-centric translation research.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: All source sentences are in English and translated by human translators, which introduces translationese effects. The authors acknowledge that translationese has known idiosyncrasies but conjecture these effects are marginal when evaluating models on low-resource languages. The sentence selection process was performed by 10 annotators (6 male, 4 female) from different regions (East Asia, South Asia, Southern Europe, Latin America, North America), which may introduce selection bias. Content is sourced from Wikipedia, which may not represent all domains or cultural perspectives equally.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Non-English source sentences are produced by human translators (translationese), which may introduce idiosyncrasies. Language coverage, while broad, does not include all world languages. Some languages considered for inclusion were unable to meet the 90% quality threshold after multiple rounds of re-translation and were excluded. The dataset is primarily suitable for evaluation rather than training due to its size. Wikipedia content may not represent all domains equally.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Primary use case is evaluation/testing of machine translation systems, particularly for low-resource and multilingual (many-to-many) translation. The dataset supports: (1) evaluation of 10,100 language pairs in many-to-many translation, (2) document-level translation evaluation, (3) multimodal translation evaluation (via image metadata), (4) sentence and document classification, (5) language identification, (6) multilingual domain adaptation. The dev split is intended for hyperparameter tuning, devtest for testing during development, and test set (available via evaluation server) for final evaluation and shared tasks such as WMT 2021 Large-Scale Multilingual Task.
